name: Bala Brahma Temple, Alampur
period: Early Chalukya, late 7th century; the one Navabrahma temple still in daily worship
summary: The largest of Alampur's nine Navabrahma temples and the only one still in daily worship, Bala Brahma keeps Shiva as Bala Brahmeshwara — and for six centuries it sheltered the goddess Jogulamba within its walls.

sections.history: Bala Brahma is the principal temple of the Navabrahma group, the nine Early Chalukya shrines raised on the Tungabhadra at Alampur in the seventh and eighth centuries, and it is the only one of them in which worship has never ceased. It is generally placed in the later seventh century. A Sanskrit inscription on one of its pillars, cut in the reign of the Chalukya king Vijayaditya (696–733), celebrates his father Vinayaditya's victory over the lord of the northern country and the seizure of the royal insignia of the kings of Malwa and Lata. The temple's later story is bound to the goddess: when the Jogulamba shrine was destroyed in 1390, her image was carried here for safety, and she was worshipped within these walls until her own temple was rebuilt beside it in 2005.
sections.architecture: The largest temple of the group and the most complete as a working shrine, Bala Brahma is built of the local sandstone, with a curving northern-style tower over the sanctum. A porch and a broad pillared hall lead to the sanctum, which is ringed by an inner passage for circumambulation, and a pillared verandah wraps the whole building so that devotees can make a second, outer round. Perforated stone windows filter light into the hall. Inside, carvings of Mahishasuramardini, the Seven Mothers, Indra and Agni line the hall, and a large dancing Shiva spreads across the ceiling; many of the outer niches now stand empty.
sections.legends: Alampur's temple names recall a tradition that Brahma performed penance here and worshipped Shiva, who is remembered in nine forms across the group; Bala Brahma, 'the youthful Brahma', is the foremost of them. Devotees say the linga in the sanctum bears the shape of a bull's hoof-print, a sign of Nandi's presence. The temple's deepest story, though, is one of shelter: for more than six hundred years it kept the goddess Jogulamba safe after her shrine was lost, and Shiva here is still worshipped as her consort, Bala Brahmeshwara.
sections.festivals: Maha Shivaratri is the temple's great night, its vigil and abhishekam drawing pilgrims from Telangana, Andhra Pradesh and Karnataka. Because Bala Brahmeshwara is worshipped as Jogulamba's consort, the temple shares in her Navaratri and Dasara celebrations and her annual Brahmotsavam, while Mondays and the month of Kartika bring steady crowds. Confirm dates locally.
sections.experience: Most pilgrims come to Bala Brahma straight from the Jogulamba temple a few steps away, completing the paired darshan of the goddess and her lord. After the sanctum, walk the outer verandah slowly and look up at the dancing Shiva on the hall ceiling. The other Navabrahma temples are only a short stroll across the lawns — Garuda Brahma just to the south, Swarga Brahma behind — and the river ghats lie close by.

visit.timings: Open daily for darshan in the morning and evening, with a midday closure; Maha Shivaratri, Navaratri and Mondays are the busiest times. Confirm current timings locally.
visit.dressCode: Modest traditional dress is expected — shoulders and knees covered; footwear is left outside before entering. As a living shrine, respectful conduct is asked of all visitors.
visit.photography: Photography is not permitted in the sanctum; follow the posted rules and the priests' guidance. The surrounding Navabrahma monuments are protected by the Archaeological Survey of India and have their own rules.
visit.gettingThere: Alampur is in Jogulamba Gadwal district, about 25 km from Kurnool and some 220 km south of Hyderabad, just off the Hyderabad–Bengaluru highway (NH 44). Alampur Road railway station, on the Hyderabad–Kurnool line, is about 9 km away, with local transport to the riverside precinct, where the temple stands beside the Jogulamba temple.
